The Northern quoll (Dasyurus hallucatus) exhibits a relatively brief gestation period of 20 days [tg = 20 days] when females are maintained under standard laboratory conditions at 35.9 °C [T = 35.9 °C]. This remarkably short intrauterine development is characteristic of many dasyurid marsupials, reflecting their reliance on a highly altricial neonatal strategy. Newborns emerge from the birth canal after this rapid developmental phase weighing just 0.0235 grams [Wwb = 0.0235 grams], a miniscule mass that allows the mother to sustain multiple offspring during the energetically demanding lactation period. The neonatal individuals, often referred to as joeys, must immediately travel from the urogenital opening to the pouch, where they attach firmly to a teat and continue their development in a protected, milk-rich environment. This extreme altriciality, with birth occurring at such an early developmental stage, imposes significant constraints on litter size and maternal energy budgets, yet it also allows the mother to quickly replace a lost litter if necessary during the brief breeding season.

Following the critical transition to life outside the pouch, the suckling juveniles remain continuously attached to the teats for the first several weeks, during which time their external features and organ systems complete development. The weaning process, marking the nutritional independence of the offspring and the cessation of lactation, begins approximately 90 days after birth [tx = approximately 90 days after birth] in captivity when the ambient temperature is held at 35.9 °C [T = 35.9 °C]. At this stage, the young quolls begin to consume solid food, primarily invertebrates and small vertebrates, and gradually reduce their reliance on maternal milk. This dietary transition represents a significant energetic shift for the growing juvenile, as they must now actively forage to meet their daily metabolic costs rather than receiving a constant supply of lipid-rich milk. The timing of weaning is critical for maternal reproductive success, as earlier weaning allows the female to regain body condition and potentially produce a second litter within the same breeding season, whereas delayed weaning may compromise her ability to reproduce again.

Sexual maturation in the Northern quoll, characterized by the onset of gonadal activity and the attainment of reproductive viability, occurs at 315 days after birth [tp = 315 days after birth] when individuals are maintained at a stable temperature of 35.9 °C [T = 35.9 °C]. This relatively early puberty, compared to larger dasyurid species, aligns well with the species' semelparous life-history strategy observed in many northern populations, where males often die shortly after their first breeding season. Young females that have completed their growth phase and achieved reproductive maturity can distinguish between the sexes, with males typically attaining a larger ultimate body size. Puberty in this species marks the beginning of a short but intense reproductive window, during which both sexes must locate mates and successfully copulate before the onset of the dry season, which brings diminished prey availability and increased physiological stress. The synchrony of oestrus among females in a population further intensifies male-male competition, driving the need for early maturation.

Adult body size in this species exhibits pronounced sexual dimorphism, a pattern common among many dasyurid carnivores. Females reach a maximum adult body mass of 690 grams [Wwi = 690 grams], a relatively modest size that facilitates their arboreal foraging habits and reduces absolute metabolic demands. In contrast, males attain a considerably larger maximum adult body mass of 1120 grams [Wwi = 1120 grams], a size advantage that confers greater success in intrasexual combat for access to receptive females during the mating season. This pronounced difference in adult body mass influences nearly every aspect of the species' ecology, from the size of prey items they can subdue to their home range dimensions and daily energetic requirements. The larger body size of males comes at a significant cost, however, as they must sustain higher absolute food intake rates and are more vulnerable to predation during periods of prey scarcity. Female body mass, meanwhile, appears to be optimized for the dual demands of successfully rearing a litter while maintaining the mobility needed to hunt effectively.

Respirometry trials conducted on adult Northern quolls have provided valuable data on the species' basal metabolic rate. At a body temperature typical of active, euthermic individuals (35.9 °C [T = 35.9 °C]), the maximum resting metabolic rate recorded was 192 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 192 milliliters of oxygen per hour], a measurement derived from a single adult individual weighing 532.3 grams. This basal oxygen consumption rate, while modest in absolute terms, is consistent with the metabolic scaling relationships observed across other medium-sized dasyurid marsupials and reflects the species' carnivorous diet and relatively high activity levels. The lifespan of this species, determined from both wild and captive records, extends to approximately 5.9 years [am = approximately 5.9 years] under controlled thermal conditions of 35.9 °C [T = 35.9 °C], though most free-living individuals succumb much earlier due to predation, disease, or the physiological collapse associated with post-mating male die-off. Reproductive output is correspondingly compressed, with females producing a maximum of approximately 6 to 7 pups per litter [N_R_i = approximately 6 to 7 pups per litter] and typically 1 litter per year [F_R_i = 1 litter per year], yielding a total annual reproductive output of roughly 6.8 pups per year when maintained at 35.9 °C [T = 35.9 °C], a rate that reflects the combined effect of average litter size and the potential for a second litter within a single season.
